# Fostering students' AI literacy development through educational games: AI knowledge, affective and cognitive engagement

### Davy Tsz Kit Ng[1](#fostering-students-ai-literacy-development-through-educational-games-ai-knowledge-affective-and-cognitive-engagement) \| Chen Xinyu[1](#fostering-students-ai-literacy-development-through-educational-games-ai-knowledge-affective-and-cognitive-engagement) \| Jac Ka Lok Leung[2](#fostering-students-ai-literacy-development-through-educational-games-ai-knowledge-affective-and-cognitive-engagement) \| Samuel Kai Wah Chu[3](#fostering-students-ai-literacy-development-through-educational-games-ai-knowledge-affective-and-cognitive-engagement)

Kong. Background: As the significance of artificial intelligence (AI) continues to increase, Email: [davyngtk@connect.hku.hk](mailto:davyngtk@connect.hku.hk) there is a need for effective scaffolding and support for novice learners. Educators

have encountered challenges in effectively scaffolding novice learners AI concepts, and providing appropriate motivational support. Research evidence has shown the potential of game-based approaches to fostering secondary school students' AI liter-

acy and motivation to learn AI.

Objectives: This study developed an online platform TreasureIsland to gamify ebooks and investigated whether and how students playing with it can effectively enhance their AI literacy. This study aims to contribute an empirical and theoretical basis for AI literacy education and promote the use of gamification that would be broadly

applied in other schools.

Methods: A quasi-experiment was conducted to evaluate the effects of the proposed gamified approach, which included a control group using an ebook with playful resources. To triangulate the quantitative results obtained from the pre and post-test,

focus group interviews were also conducted.

Results: The platform was effective in improving students' motivation, self-efficacy, career interest, and understanding of AI concepts and ethics, but did not enhance their confidence of using AI, and high cognition of applying, evaluating and creating AI. TreasureIsland players demonstrated significant improvement in all affective and cognitive domains, except for the ability to apply, evaluate, and create AI. Interviews revealed that the gamified approach could promote students' AI literacy by adhering to guidelines, including (1) creating a competitive and motivating learning environ- ment through game mechanics, (2) providing scaffolding modules and feedback, and

3. visualising complex AI concepts via simulations. Feedback collected from the study suggested adding pedagogical elements such as flipped classrooms and project-based

Conclusions: This study concludes that the use of gamification can provide affective and cognitive support and an enjoyable experience for fostering learners' AI literacy. It helps instructional designers and teachers enrich the pedagogical knowledge

related to gamified platform and AI literacy.

### 2 \| LITERATURE REVIEW

To address the learning challenges of AI literacy and develop an effec- tive instructional design, this section first presents existing curricula and identifies challenges of learning AI. Second, the idea of educa- tional tools for fostering students' AI literacy was examined, and gami- fication is further discussed to understand possible design principles that inform educators of effective approaches to develop AI literacy instruction.

### 2.1 \| AI literacy

Existing studies have explored what secondary students should learn about AI (e.g., Kandlhofer et al., 2016; Chiu et al., [2021;](#8--conclusions) Furey & Martin, 2019; Williams et al., 2023). Many initiatives, policies, curric- ula and teaching guidelines provide frameworks to suggest the age- appropriate topic areas of K-12 AI curricula. For example, Touretzky et al. (2019) organised discrete AI knowledge and skills as the five big ideas in the AIK12 initiative, including perception, representation and reasoning, learning, natural interaction, and societal impact. UNESCO (2022) covered three major categories, including AI foundations; ethics and social impact; and understanding, using and developing AI. Chiu et al. ([2021)](#8--conclusions) designed an AI curriculum framework that includes introduction and fundamentals to AI; how AI sees, hears, speaks and reads; AI reasoning, simulating, thinking and creating; social good, social impacts and challenges of AI, AI and ethics, and AI and future of work. Casal-Otero et al. ([2023)](#8--conclusions) discussed learning tech- nical, conceptual, and applied skills in a specific domain of interest, with a particular focus on efforts to design models that frame AI liter- acy proposals.

While these frameworks are promising, they tend to prioritise instructional content over learning environments and pedagogies that support students' needs. According to prior research, students often face affective and cognitive challenges. Students feel bored and

distracted and lose motivation in complex concepts, such as neural networks and AI algorithms (Long et al., 2021; Ng et al., 2021). Sec- ond, it is challenging for novice learners to learn AI without prior knowledge due to its high-level abstractions, and lack scaffolding sup- port to learn AI (Casal-Otero et al., [2023;](#8--conclusions) Ng, Leung, et al., 2023). It also involves students' high cognition levels of AI learning, including critical thinking, and problem-solving in real-world context (Yang, 2022), collaboration with AI, and creativity (Taddeo & Floridi, 2018). Tedre et al. (2021) described the challenges that students face in AI literacy courses, such as the shift from rule-based to data-driven environments, and the need for age-appropriate pedagogical entry points.

Ng et al. (2021) adapted Bloom's taxonomy and categorised AI curriculum contents from low to high-order thinking tendency. Based on the model, students should achieve (1) the ability to know and understand basic AI concepts; (2) apply, evaluate and create AI appli- cations; and equip with (3) the ethical competence that critically eval- uate AI in different situations. This study is based on this model to examine students’ cognitive engagement.

### 2.2 \| Tools for developing AI literacy

Nowadays, there are more age-appropriate tools that help students develop students' AI concepts, and engage students in experiencing how to develop machine learning models without programming knowledge. For example, Touretzky et al. (2019) identified some edu- cational tools such as Teachable Machine, Quickdraw, and Scratch extension that raise students' interest in creating their own AI crea- tions. Voulgari et al. (2021) developed Artbot that uses a constructiv- ist approach to introduce secondary students to AI learning content, providing opportunities for exploration, experimentation, and reflec- tion. Pope et al. (2023) surpassed Google's Teachable Machine to develop GenAI Teachable Machine, which enabled students to link classifier results to actions using text, sound, and pictures. Other AI applications such as ChatGPT-empowered bots, Google AI experi- ments, and Moral Machine are also publicly available for students and are recommended in the ebook to familiarise young learners with AI technologies, experiment with machine learning models, and gain practical insights into the workings of AI mechanisms (Ali et al., [2022;](#8--conclusions) Formosa & Ryan, 2021; Kasneci et al., 2023; Vartiainen et al., 2020). With these AI technologies, young learners can communicate with AI via natural language and computer vision technologies, without prior programming experience (Vartiainen et al., 2020).

Developing AI literacy involves not only understanding technical concepts, but also being able to apply them in real-world contexts, and complement with other high order thinking skills (e.g., creativity, evaluation). With teaching tools, teachers can incorporate develop- mentally appropriate experiences to attract students to learn AI, and promote deeper understanding of AI concepts. Further, these tools provide students with opportunities to conceptualise and experiment with AI, as well as reflect on what they have learned through experi- ential learning (Hsu et al., 2023). Moreover, students can learn how to

collaborate with their peers in an AI-empowered environment through project-based activities, which aligns with sociocultural learning (Vartiainen et al., 2020) and design-oriented and collaborative peda- gogy (Vartiainen et al., 2021). The tools also help alleviate cognitive challenges and promote the development of higher-order thinking skills, including interdisciplinary thinking, collaboration, critical think- ing, and real-world problem-solving (Sakulkueakulsuk et al., 2018; Henry et al., 2021).

### 2.3 \| Gamification

Gamification is the process of incorporating game mechanics and design principles to non-game contexts. It refers to the incorporation of gaming mechanics, such as points, badges, challenges, leader boards, honours, and incentives, into educational contexts to motivate students to engage more deeply and meaningfully (Werbach et al., 2012). Gamification for education is based on the notion that well-designed games can inspire increases in learner efficiency and creativity (Flores, 2015). The MDE model is considered as one of the most effective mechanisms for transferring games into non-game con- texts. The three elements of design that make gamification effective are mechanics (M), dynamics (D), and emotions (E) (Robson et al., 2015). Teachers adopt MDE to satisfy students' needs that drive learning behaviours by providing its goals, environments, interactions, and rules. The motivational nature of the gamified experience could result in game dynamics that satisfy learners' desire for reward, achievement, and competition. Such gamified dynamics can cause par- ticipants to feel a variety of emotions, such as interest, motivation, self-efficacy and satisfaction, confidence in overcoming a challenge, disappointment, and anxiety (Robson et al., 2015). Using MDE can cultivate students' digital literacy (Reynolds, 2016), which also sheds light on the potential to develop students' AI literacy.

Given the complexity of and the prerequisite technical back- ground knowledge required to comprehend AI, it is challenging to learn AI, especially for K-12 students (Bennani et al., [2022)](#8--conclusions). Since there remains a lack of empirical studies exploring the specific roles of gamification in enhancing AI literacy among students, we further added game elements such as challenges, rewards, and feedback in a gamified platform called TreasureIsland as an intervention. By doing so, we aim to make the learning experience more engaging and inter- active to meet students' affective and cognitive needs, potentially increasing student motivation and improving AI learning outcomes.

### 3 \| INSTRUCTIONAL DESIGN

Two learning environments, TreasureIsland and ebook, were devel- oped to enhance students' AI literacy in affective and cognitive domains. TreasureIsland is a hands-on platform based on the success- ful gamified platform called Reading Battle, while ebook includes videos, learning tools, readings, and practice activities. Gamified chal- lenges are completed after lessons in TreasureIsland. Table S1 displays the features of each learning environment used in the study.

TreasureIsland is based on the successful platform that includes sci- ence and language learning resources with reference to the Robson's MDE model (Qiao et al., 2023).

The units cover foundational AI concepts, practical skills, and AI ethics. Each module includes reading materials, videos, tools, and gamification tasks to help students understand AI. Later modules include high-order thinking activities to help students apply AI tech- niques and explore different AI tools for analysis, creation, and pro- ductivity. Appendix S1 displays 10 learning units based on the Ng et al. (2021) framework for teaching AI literacy. Ethical principles such as fairness, accountability, and transparency are also introduced to promote responsible AI literacy.

### 3.1 \| Ebook in control group

For the control group, we utilised an ebook platform that included learning activities from the AI literacy curriculum, with the intended learning outcomes presented in Appendix S1. To ensure student engagement, we selected teaching tools that aligned with Montazami et al. (2022) five criteria: curriculum, development team, feedback, scaffolding, and pedagogical approach. For instance, we incorporated AI-for-Ocean from [Code.org,](http://code.org) which was designed to captivate stu- dents by involving them in the creation of simple ML models to clean the ocean. The activities within this tool have clearly defined learning goals, such as using AI to address ocean pollution, and complement the units covered in the AI curriculum. Second, this tool was devel- oped by a team of experts, and previous research has shown its effec- tiveness in catering to students' developmental abilities (Martins et al., 2023; Qiao et al., 2023; Williams et al., 2023). To provide guid- ance and support, the tool offers real-time feedback to steer students towards making the correct choices. The tool includes scaffolding ele- ments like reading resources, scenarios, videos, animations, and music/sound. As students make progress through the tool, they are gradually introduced to more challenging tasks, such as identifying and categorising fish shapes while distinguishing between garbage and actual fish. Lastly, this teaching artefact can be implemented within pedagogical frameworks such as project-based learning and experiential learning (Martins et al., 2023; Williams et al., 2023).

Other tools, including QuickDraw, Teachable Machine, Moral Machine, and Google AI Experiments, were also chosen to provide students with an engaging learning experience to learn AI conceptual and practical content. The choices of these tools in the ebook were based on learners' cognitive development, and the instructions enable students to play at their own pace after school (Figure 1). Quizzes were provided at the end of the module to enable students to practice their AI knowledge.

### 4 \| METHODS

This case study employed a mixed-methods design and conducted a quasi-experiment to compare student outcomes in terms of tested AI

FIGURE 3a Multiple-choice challenges in

each learning module.

FIGURE 3b Learning summary and details.

knowledge, affective and cognitive engagement between the Treasur- eIsland treatment group and ebook control group (Creswell & Plano Clark, [2018)](#8--conclusions).

### 4.1 \| Participants

For the quantitative phase, we recruited two classes of Secondary 1 (Grade 7) students from a secondary school in Hong Kong. The school has students with a range of socio-economic backgrounds. By random assignment, one class was assigned to use an ebook to learn AI (N = 33, control group) whereas another class used TreasureIsland (N = 35, treatment group). Although all students indicated that they have heard of AI and have some experience in using AI in their daily life, they have no prior knowledge about AI. To triangulate the

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

FIGURE 4 Experimental procedure.

quantitative results obtained from the pre and post-test, focus group interviews were conducted. All students from the treatment group were invited to the interviews. We obtained the approval from their institutions, parents and students in the research.

### 4.2 \| Instruments

Pre-test questionnaires were used to gather demographic information and measure students' baseline self-reported affective and cognitive engagement about learning AI (Appendix S2). Post-test questionnaires were given at the end of the last lesson to measure the effectiveness of the ebook and TreasureIsland. The questionnaire was validated in a previous study with an overall Cronbach's alpha value of 0.91 (Ng et al., 2024). Follow-up interviews were conducted with teachers, students, and experts to ensure questionnaire reliability.

We designed an AI knowledge test (Appendix S3) with multiple- choice questions of similar difficulty to the TreasureIsland and ebook quizzes. The questions focus on recalling basic AI knowledge, applying and evaluating concepts, and knowing ethical principles. The questions were designed based on the ebook content and guidelines for designing multiple-choice questions, and were verified as relevant by teachers.

Focus group interviews were conducted with students to elaborate their views on the gamified platform and ebook design, and how gamifi- cation offers knowledge, affective and cognitive support to develop their AI literacy (Appendix S4). These topics can help better understand students' learning experiences and triangulate the quantitative results. The interviews help to understand how the elements of TreasureIsland and ebook can influence students' lower to higher order thinking skills.

### 4.3 \| Procedures and data analysis

The learning intervention consists of warm-up, direct instruction, hands-on and after-school activities that spanned across two months

with 10 sessions lasting 35 min per session (Figure [4)](#42--instruments). Students were provided with either online or gamified quizzes after each module and both types of quizzes were made up of six questions with a game rule to calculate the final score. Basic AI understandings were discussed in lessons 1–4, and practical lessons were held during lessons 5–10, and lesson 2, 4–6, and 8–10 covered materials related to AI ethics in dif- ferent scenarios or areas. With the use of questionnaires and inter- view protocols, the intervention activities were evaluated at the end of the programme.

Students in the treatment group took gamified quizzes while those in the control group had ebook learning instruction with online quizzes. To eliminate confounding factors, both ebook and Treasur- eIsland conditions were conducted by the same teacher and had identical instruction length, structure, and content. At the end of the lesson, students took about 10 min to complete the online AI literacy questionnaires. As suggested by prior studies, student engagement is a multidimensional concept with affective, behavioural, and cogni- tive engagement (Hong et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2022;Ng et al.,2024). This study focused on affective and cognitive engagement, which is related to students' psychological investment and cognitive development.

All quantitative data was analysed using nonparametric tests due to the data not satisfying the assumptions of normal distribution (Kruskal, 1952). Paired-sample nonparametric tests were used to examine learning improvements, and independent samples nonpara- metric tests were employed to compare groups. The correlation between AI knowledge, affective and cognitive engagement was ana- lysed with Spearman's nonparametric correlation.

Qualitative data was collected through semi-structured interviews and analysed using thematic analysis in Monkeylearn software, which is specifically designed for sentiment analysis. The software used tex- tual analysis models to automatically tag the data, including sentiment and identify key themes (Sadriu et al., 2021). With the themes sug- gested by the software, students' dialogues were further categorised by first and second author with an inter-rater test conducted to

ensure coding accuracy, with a high inter-rater reliability 85% (Hallgren, 2012).

### 5 \| RESULTS

### 5.1 \| Improvement of learning outcomes (RQ1)

First, the pre- and post-test scores were compared to investigate the change of the students' level of engagement. Mann–Whitney U tests on the pretest scores showed no statistically significant difference between the two groups on any of the measures (p \> 0.05). There- fore, both groups were considered equal in terms of their prior knowl- edge of the AI content and levels of engagement.

A nonparametric test was used since the data was not normally distributed (p \< 0.05 in the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test and skewed histograms). Therefore, Wilcoxon signed-rank test (a nonparametric equivalent of the dependent t-test) was used when the assumptions had been violated and the use of the dependent t-test is inappropriate (Çakıroglu et al., [2017)](#8--conclusions). The test results showed a significant improve- ment from the pre- to post-test results for affective engagement (Table S3), cognitive engagement and AI knowledge (Table S4).

In the ebook group, the mean scores of the post-test have improved in intrinsic motivation, and self-efficacy (p \< 0.05), except for career interest and confidence, which showed a marginally signifi- cant improvement (p = 0.05). With regards to cognitive engagement, there was a significant improvement of the two cognitive domains (i.e., know and understand; apply, evaluate and create), AI ethics, and AI knowledge. The results of the TreasureIsland group indicated that students significantly improved in all of the affective constructs. Simi- lar to the ebook group, TreasureIsland players showed improvements in the two cognitive domains, AI ethics, and AI knowledge.

### 5.2 \| Effects of the gamified approach compared to ebook (RQ2)

Nonparametric Mann–Whitney U tests were carried out to com- pare students' post-affective and cognitive engagement between the TreasureIsland and ebook groups. The results, as shown in Table S5, indicated a statistically significant difference between the two groups for intrinsic motivation, self-efficacy, career inter- est, and confidence (p ≤ 0.01). Table S6 showed a significant dif- ference in the lower cognition ‘know and understand’ construct between the gamification in TreasureIsland and ebook (p \< 0.05). Although students in the TreasureIsland group had a higher mean score for ‘apply, evaluate, and create’, there was no statistically significant difference between the two groups (p = 0.90 \> 0.05). In terms of AI ethics, there was a statistically significant differ- ence between the two conditions. This suggests that gamification had a stronger effect in developing students' AI ethics (p \< 0.01) by helping them understand the limitations and ethical principles behind AI.

Mann–Whitney U tests result on the post-test AI knowledge revealed a statistically significant difference between ebook and TreasureIsland (p \> 0.05), indicating that students who played Treas- ureIsland can have a better AI knowledge. It appears that both instruc- tional methods are effective in enhancing students' AI literacy. The second RQ suggests that the proposed TreasureIsland approach is more effective in promoting students' affective and cognitive engage- ment, and enhancing their tested AI knowledge.

### 5.3 \| Relations between engagement and AI knowledge

To verify the relationships between affective and cognitive engage- ment, and AI knowledge, Spearman's nonparametric correlation was employed. The three constructs were calculated based on the average of their sub-variables. Figure [5](#612--self-efficacy-of-learning-ai) indicates that some of the learning outcomes were significantly correlated with each other. This suggests that self-reported engagement is not a one-dimensional construct, but rather a multidimensional measure of learner engagement in AI liter- acy education. Acronyms referred to in the notes below Figure [5,](#612--self-efficacy-of-learning-ai) the test demonstrates that the AK, KU and EC of the participants were considerably close, and the four affective domains (IM, CI, SE, CO) were also associated with each other. In other words, students having high AI knowledge also had high self-reported AI literacy in terms of knowledge and understanding. Interestingly, AE, CI, SE and IM were particularly related, and CO and AK have close relations. That is, stu- dents are morally better, the more motivated they are to demonstrate ethical thoughts and actions. Students having better AI knowledge were more likely to be more confident of learning AI.

### 6 \| QUALITATIVE PHASE

To understand how gamification affected students' engagement and AI knowledge, the transcripts from the focus-group interviews were analysed. Based on the qualitative data, some possible explanations for the improvement in engagement and AI knowledge were sug- gested. Figure [6](#612--self-efficacy-of-learning-ai) presented students' perspectives about the positive, negative and neutral themes for their AI literacy development.

### 6.1 \| Affective engagement

### 6.1.1 \| Learning motivation

Twenty-seven students reported that the game design motivated them to construct knowledge and perform practical tasks. First, playful experiences in the ebook were found to enhance affective engagement. Twenty-four students felt motivated when carrying out task-based activities in the ebook. For example, student responses were: ‘Initially, I think AI is difficult to learn, but this game raises my interest to learn AI through playing’ and ‘The tools recommended in

understand; EC = Apply, evaluate & create; AE = AI ethics; AK = AI

knowledge.

FIGURE 6 Students' perspectives on AI literacy development.

this ebook make me curious about how AI works’. The choices of tasks are important to enhance students' motivation. It brings stu- dents fun, enjoyable, interesting, and motivating learning experiences, which supports the quantitative findings showing significant improve- ments in intrinsic motivation.

TreasureIsland students claimed the effectiveness of game mechanics to enhance their motivation, thus improving their perfor- mance. This platform offers roles in a storyline, leaderboard, and badges to enhance their motivation of learning AI, thus enabling stu- dents to explore more tasks. Students were motivated by the chance to achieve a place on the leaderboard, which was an entertaining and competitive experience. At the end of each week, students would be excited to know who the top 20 students were. Comments from the

interviews confirmed the idea: ‘The platform encourages us to com- pete with our classmates. … Everyone sustained to learn AI after school and tried not to miss any challenges in the platform.’ Students also reported on the use of other game elements to sustain AI learn- ing. For example, a student stated: ‘We wanted to get promoted and gained more badges. It made the gamified tasks more interesting and authentic.’

### 6.1.2 \| Self-efficacy of learning AI

Both groups of students demonstrated an improvement in their self- efficacy, which refers to their belief in their capacity to successfully

complete specific AI learning tasks. Being listed on the leaderboard could enhance students' self-efficacy of learning AI. The rankings were placed up to 20. Students who were initially performing at a lower level of achievement were motivated to improve when they realised they had the potential to climb the leaderboard. Eight middle- achieved students found this experience valuable because they believed it was possible to improve their skills. The player's profile enabled students to monitor their progress and measure their achievement, and the leaderboard enabled them to compare their efforts and task completion with their classmates.

Twenty-five students reported that TreasureIsland enhances their self-efficacy of learning AI and confidence of using AI. First, Treasur- eIsland provided clear scaffolding structure, and levels of difficulties to develop students' AI literacy from lower to higher cognition. Twenty students reported that scaffolding structure helped them develop a belief in their ability to succeed in AI learning tasks. Inter- viewees reported that this structure helped them achieve their goals in AI learning by making incremental progress. A student acknowl- edged, ‘The supports guide us to succeed in more tasks, and the con- tent is designed based on what we have learnt.’

Other supports such as badges, hints, second attempts, and feed- back could also improve students' self-efficacy of learning AI. Students highlighted the benefits of these elements: ‘The platform gave me second attempts when I got a wrong answer. It provided hints that helped me build confidence to try more challenging ques- tions.’ and ‘I feel confident that I will do well in the AI tasks when gaining more badges.’ Overall, these game elements encouraged stu- dents to persevere in AI learning when faced with difficulties.

### 6.1.3 \| Confidence in using AI

Confidence in using AI in everyday life differs from self-efficacy in learning AI, as students apply what they have learned to solve daily problems beyond the textbook. In the ebook, some students lacked confidence in performing AI-related tasks, such as data analysis and decision-making based on AI suggestions. Without persistence in learning, students felt unable to apply their AI knowledge to real-life situations. Moreover, some students found it difficult to use AI devices and applications. As a student explained: ‘I can't follow the complex procedures to create my own projects’. In contrast, Treasur- eIsland learners were more confident in using AI due to their knowl- edge retention through gamification. Gamifying AI literacy enables learners to practice more and explore more about AI from different angles after lessons, which make them gain more practical AI under- standing. A student commented on the benefits of gamification: ‘I feel more confident in selecting appropriate tools to solve problems in dif- ferent scenarios.’

### 6.1.4 \| Career interest

Developing career interest is important to prepare students with ade- quate AI competencies to sustain their AI learning after graduation.

Eighteen students claimed that TreasureIsland could enable them to explore various applications of AI in different fields, and understand potential career paths and opportunities about AI. Gamification pro- vides students with opportunities for skill development and practical experience. They could acquire and apply skills in areas, such as data analysis, task automation, and multimedia processing, which are useful for their future study and job. Exemplary responses were: ‘People who know AI will replace people who don't. Learning AI will give me a career advantage and benefit my future career,’ and ‘My future career and study will involve AI, not just computer scientists’. These com- ments reinforce the quantitative findings that suggest gamification has a more positive impact on students’ career interests.

### 6.2 \| Cognitive engagement

### 6.2.1 \| Know and understand

Twenty-seven students reported that the task-based activities enabled them to construct AI knowledge. It was found that both the ebook and TreasureIsland interventions effectively improved students tested and self-reported AI knowledge and understandings. For ebooks, games provided a supportive environment for experimenta- tion and visualisation of complex AI concepts. Students were able to develop practical skills and learn from their mistakes while completing tasks like generating ML models and stylising images. In TreasureIs- land, gamified elements were further incorporated into the ebook to address the challenges of learning AI. The structured and guided learning experience broke down complex concepts into modules and gamified practices, making it easier for students to understand the material. The platform also encouraged students' motivation through positive competitions and gamified experiences. Instant feedback and recognition further built cognitive support for continued learning. Stu- dents claimed, ‘The materials are appropriate and enable me to get the key ideas about AI’ and ‘The modules in the platform make com- plicated AI concepts into smaller, and more manageable chunks.’

Other students stated, ‘I realised that gamification can be an effective way to enhance my AI understanding. Before attending the workshops, I had no knowledge about AI. After the workshops, I have gained an understanding that AI involves building ML models, and the use of data for object/voice recognition.’

### 6.2.2 \| Evaluate and create

Students' abilities to evaluate and create AI were not enhanced by either TreasureIsland or the ebook. Several potential issues were sug- gested by the students. First, the tasks in the ebook and gamified plat- form were found to be ‘black-boxed’, with students following instructions without fully understanding the underlying principles. While students could use AI tools to complete tasks, they did not understand the concepts and algorithmic thinking behind them. Creat- ing and evaluating AI requires technical expertise in mathematics, pro- gramming, and data analysis. However, at their current level, students

may only know the basic working principles. This leaves room for stu- dents to continue learning AI as they grow and learn more advanced AI-related mathematics and computer principles. A student commen- ted, ‘There is still much AI knowledge I can't understand. I think I may learn it in the future.’

Second, students raised time constraints as an issue. They sug- gested extending lesson times to allow for more hands-on experience. AI learning involves many practical skills, and creating and evaluating AI artefacts, such as machine learning model building, can be time- consuming. Teachers often prepare semi-finished or designated prod- ucts, limiting students' ability to create their own work. Even in the gamification condition, evaluating and creating involves high-order thinking, and self-paced learning in the gamified platform may not enable students to reach the cognitive level required.

Third, a teacher proposed the use of project-based learning that helps students build collaboration, critical thinking and problem- solving skills through co-creation and competitions (e.g., learn how to work together using AI tools, collaborate with AI in a competition as a team, and solve real-world problems together using AI). A teacher sug- gested, ‘Using the gamified flipped classroom approach can help stu- dents study basic concepts at home before attending in-person lessons to learn advanced skills. This would allow for more lesson time to engage students in project-based learning and hands-on activities, while reducing direct instruction time.’ These suggestions highlight the need for a cognitive and structured approach to teaching AI, focusing on understanding the underlying principles and providing students with sufficient time and scaffolding support to develop their AI literacy.

### 6.2.3 \| AI ethics

Twenty-three students appreciated the use of TreasureIsland to gamify ebook content to develop their AI ethics. Ebook offers a fault-tolerant environment to explore AI ethical issues, such as pri- vacy, bias, and fairness, through simulation games that challenge them to think critically about the concerns and limitations behind AI technologies. A student mentioned, ‘… Teachers further lead discussions of ethical principles with students. The ebook can include a set of these tasks for us to think about the ethical con- cerns behind AI.’

During their interviews, students suggested that gamifying AI ethics could provide opportunities to practice various ethical prin- ciples related to AI and encourage critical thinking about the topic. For example, they suggested the importance of ‘transparency when using AI for decision-making’, ‘avoiding bias and discrimina- tion’, ‘protecting the data privacy and security of AI systems’, ‘addressing human values instead of prioritising efficiency and profit’, and ‘demonstrating social responsibility’ via gamified prac- tices in TreasureIsland. AI ethics is not simply knowing these rules and recalling the meanings of ethical principles; gamification encourages students to evaluate and think critically about the potential hazards behind AI applications.

### 7 \| DISCUSSION

This study indicates that gamifying AI literacy has a positive effect on students' affective and cognitive engagement. The discussion section is constructed in three subsections focusing on the effect of gamification elements on student affective and cognitive engagement, and relation between gamification, student engagement, and aca- demic performance. The section aims to provide insights to practi- tioners on effective instructional design and strategies on gamifying AI literacy based on this experience.

### 7.1 \| Gamification as an affective support

AI concepts may pose learning challenges for young learners due to a disparity between their everyday experiences and the abstract nature of AI concepts. Through playful experiences, students can sustain their motivation when playing TreasureIsland than when learning with an ebook. By leveraging game mechanics, students could compete with their peers, earn digital badges and points, reach higher leader- board positions based on a storyline, all of which help their retention. They feel more connected to what they have learnt and stay focused on their learning.

As suggested by recent research, AI education aims to develop students to become literates rather than consumers (e.g., Chiu et al., [2021;](#8--conclusions) Ng et al., 2021; Xia et al., 2022). We argue that Treasur- eIsland begins to achieve this goal in a way by giving students the opportunity to set their own goals and complete tasks on the plat- form. Gamified platforms like TreasureIsland could gamify AI concepts and served as a starting point to motivate students to become ready to learn AI (Hsu et al., 2021; Ng & Chu, 2021).

In particular, TreasureIsland listed students' names on the leaderboard and gave additional points for challenging questions. Leaderboard was one of the most prominent game elements that engage students in learning (Zainuddin et al., 2020). It announced the top 15 students on the leaderboard and led to a controllable competition and points could help determine whether students are more active than their peers. Well-designed gamified platforms should offer modules that give students autonomy and choice in their learning, allowing them to take ownership of their AI literacy development and explore topics that interest them (Li & Chu, 2021). Providing timely and constructive feedback can help students reflect their responses in the tasks, and encourages them to continue learning and exploring (Qiao et al., 2023). Attali and Arieli-Attali ([2015)](#8--conclusions) found that using multiple gamification tech- niques motivates student learning. This includes providing motiva- tion, vicarious experiences, social persuasion, and emotional support. Gamification can help students feel confident in learning AI and provide a scaffolding environment for hands-on tasks. Challenging tasks build on foundational knowledge and enable stu- dents to experiment with AI applications. The platform also offers real-world scenarios to enable students to discover how AI is used in authentic settings (Ng, Leung, et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2011).

To enhance students' career interest, by gamifying hands-on AI practices in various industries, such as gaming, creativity, and environ- mental protection, students can explore career paths such as data analyst, ML engineer, and AI researcher. Gamification has been shown to improve student performance and confidence in AI learning through positive competitive and motivating environments with lead- erboards, badges, and points, which aligns with prior studies (Huang & Hew, 2018; Lo & Hew, 2020).

### 7.2 \| Gamification as a cognitive support

TreasusreIsland players had better AI knowledge and cognitive engagement than those who learned with ebooks only due to the platform's scaffolding supports and gamified content (Qiao et al., 2023). Students found the ebook contents challenging and diffi- cult to sustain learning without teacher support, whereas TreasureIs- land encouraged after-school learning through gamification.

Gamification has the potential to facilitate students' self- regulated learning using game elements (Landers et al., 2017; Qiao et al., 2023). Students could compare the level they were on and the total points they had to their peers. When students reached a new level and achieved particular rewards and badges, it could credit them for what they had accomplished. Ebook did not have the same structure, as there were no rewards and levels. It was difficult to constantly keep track of their progress (Zainuddin et al., 2020). Leaderboard recorded the points that the students gained, providing timely feedback and cognitive hints of their per- formance (Jong et al., 2018; Zainuddin, 2018). With the profile provided by the leaderboard, students could monitor their pro- gress, which encourages them to sustain their effort. It enabled students to see that they can manage more advanced AI concepts by showing them the progress of other classmates via positive competition.

Gamification can reduce cognitive challenges for novice learners studying technologically driven content, such as AI, by leveraging visual attractiveness and interactive simulations (Darejeh et al., 2021; Kim & Shim, 2022; Su & Zhong, 2022). Gamification can improve stu- dents' understanding of AI concepts through visual indicators of pro- gress, clear objectives and goals, and immediate feedback. Competitions can also boost motivation and build a sense of commu- nity. Guided learning structures can break down complex AI concepts into modules, making it easier for students to scaffold and digest the material (Kim & Shim, 2022).

To become AI literate, students should not only focus on basic knowledge and ethical principles, but also critically evaluate AI- generated responses and collaborate with AI to solve problems (Borenstein & Howard, [2021;](#8--conclusions) Furey & Martin, 2019). However, no significant differences were found in higher-level cognition between pre- and post-interventions for both approaches, possibly due to the use of multiple-choice questions and learning tasks. Interviews sug- gested that authentic, project-based, and problem-solving elements should be adopted to encourage learners to apply what they have

learned to solve real-world problems and foster creativity and collaboration.

### 7.3 \| Relations between engagement and AI knowledge

The study found that affective engagement sub-variables were corre- lated with each other, with high motivation associated with high career interest, self-efficacy, and confidence. Similarly, AI knowledge was linked to both lower and higher-order cognitive skills, indicating that students with stronger thinking skills tended to perform better in AI knowledge. These findings align with prior research indicating that affective and cognitive factors are interrelated, and students with higher cognitive engagement tend to perform better (Çakıroglu et al., [2017;](#8--conclusions) Hanus & Fox, 2015; Ng & Chu, 2021). Additionally, stu- dents with higher confidence in using AI had better AI knowledge, highlighting the importance of building students' confidence to improve their AI literacy.

AI ethics is correlated with affective domains, as ethical decision- making and behavioural outcomes are influenced by people's affective reactions to situations. Our interviews with students revealed that empathy and inclusiveness can inform ethical views on AI, with stu- dents providing examples of how AI can assist visually impaired indi- viduals. This aligns with recent research that links ethics and motivation to the inherent reason for behaving morally (Schaltegger & Burritt, 2018; Young & Durwin, 2013).

### 7.4 \| Practical implications and contributions of the study

The significance of this study can be understood in two aspects. First, it is crucial to examine the specific approach of gamification in the context of AI literacy education. The findings of this study suggest that gamifying learning experiences is not only beneficial in traditional subject areas but also in AI literacy education (Qiao et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2021). Furthermore, the complex and technical nature of AI requires a unique exploration to determine the effectiveness of gami- fication in fostering AI literacy among young learners. Gamifying ebooks for AI learning can enhance students' motivation, self-efficacy, career interest, confidence, and lower-level cognitive skills through elements such as competition and scaffolding.

Second, this study is part of our design-based research that aims to investigate effective learning strategies to motivate students to sustain their AI learning at home, thus allowing for more in-class time for engaging in maker projects within a flipped classroom setting (Qiao et al., 2023). Recent studies in AI education have demonstrated the effectiveness of playful experiences in enhancing AI literacy through immersive scenarios, case-based discussions using role- playing games, and guidance and feedback provided through AR- based games (Deng et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2023). These studies assessed students' performance on tasks that required them to

FIGURE 7 Affective and cognitive domains (adapted from Ng et al.,

acquire AI knowledge and understanding, evaluate and apply AI appli- cations, and critically reflect on AI ethics, providing a comprehensive measure of AI literacy abilities beyond basic comprehension. How- ever, there remains a dearth of studies examining the use of gamifica- tion in AI education. This study addresses this gap by focusing specifically on the context of AI education and evaluating the impact of gamifying AI knowledge. It lays the foundation for subsequent phases of our design-based research, and provides evidence to show the effects of the proposed gamified ebook platform. Overall, the gamification of AI literacy holds promise for generating new research insights as it motivates students to acquire AI knowledge and skills at home, thereby allowing for more in-class time to foster the develop- ment of higher-level cognitive skills such as creativity and problem- solving in authentic projects.

The first pedagogical implication of this article is related to the learning content and pedagogical effectiveness. Educators that plan to incorporate AI at different levels might learn from this study to choose appropriate AI content for their students when designing instruction and curriculum. When designing school-based AI literacy curriculum, educators may have difficulty in motivating students to learn and scaf- folding their cognition. This study can expect gamification platforms like TreasureIsland to help alleviate such issues. The study encouraged the use of gamification to provide students' affective and cognitive support that add values on top of the ebook design that consists of videos, reading materials and game-based approaches (e.g., puzzle games, reasoning strategy games, robot games). Through gamifying an ebook, this study shows the importance of adopting game elements

2024).

to foster students' learning motivation, basic understanding of AI knowledge and ethics. Future research can draw from our study to examine the effects of various learning contents, pedagogies and teaching tools for fostering the learning effects of using and applying AI, evaluating and creating AI, and understanding AI ethics.

Second, this study contributed to AI education research by pro- posing the meaningful measure of AI literacy development through considering affective dimensions (i.e., motivation, self-efficacy, confi- dence, career interest), and cognitive dimensions in which students gain AI knowledge and understandings, evaluate and apply AI applica- tions, and critically reflect on AI ethics. This study proposes the addi- tion of the affective domains in our existing cognition-oriented AI literacy framework (Figure 7). Future research could use measurement tools (i.e., AI literacy questionnaire, interview protocols) as references to examine students' AI literacy learning outcomes. Finally, since TreasureIsland was developed as a prototype for the experiment and had rooms for improvement, future efforts should be directed to developing a game that incorporates project-based elements with greater motivational affordances and content that is richer and more diverse.

While the study may not be groundbreaking in terms of advanc- ing gamification research specifically, it could still offer meaningful contributions to the field of AI education. Since applying game mecha- nisms to AI education is a less explored area, this article incorporated gamification elements and playful tasks into an ebook to make learn- ing about AI more engaging and accessible for students. The key value of this study may lie in demonstrating how gamification techniques

and playful experiences in the ebook can be leveraged to enhance their AI literacy and understanding of AI concepts. In that sense, the focus is less on pushing the boundaries of gamification theory, and more on developing effective instructional approaches for teaching AI.

### 8 \| CONCLUSIONS

AI literacy has become an essential component of digital literacy, and schools are designing pedagogies to address learning challenges and develop students' necessary competencies. Gamification has been recognised as a successful pedagogical strategy across disciplines. This study concludes that the use of gamification can provide affective and cognitive support and an enjoyable experience for learners. Recom- mendations for educators are listed in Appendix S5.

However, this study has some limitations. First, the sample size of this study was small. Future studies could involve larger samples. Second, while this paper mainly focuses on self-reported affective and cognitive engagement, future studies should investi- gate actual dimensions of learning that employ more comprehen- sive learning about AI, including the actual knowledge and skills of using AI applications (e.g., interacting with sensors, learning analyt- ics). Third, this article does not adopt a novel approach to teach students about AI, which may weaken the significance of this study as there have been many existing studies examining gamifi- cation in educational settings. Even if the study does not intro- duce a groundbreaking new approach, it could still have value in exploring the application of existing pedagogical strategies, like gamification, to the domain of AI education. To address the chal- lenges of teaching AI literacy education, it is important for future researchers to continue exploring other innovative approaches to
